blocks.text:
Design the autocomplete, or typeahead, feature underneath a search box, the small dropdown of suggestions that appears and updates with every single keystroke as someone types. This looks deceptively simple, but it hides a genuinely interesting constraint: it has to be fast enough that it feels instant on every keystroke, not just on the final, completed search, and the suggestions it offers need to be ranked by what people actually search for, not just by what strings happen to exist somewhere in a dictionary.

The idea that makes this fast is doing almost all of the hard work ahead of time, offline, rather than at request time. Every node in a trie of known query prefixes has its own top suggestions precomputed and cached directly on that node, so answering a live request is nothing more than walking down to the right node and reading off what is already sitting there.

blocks.text: Given a prefix a user has typed so far, the system should return a small number of the most relevant completions, ranked by how often people actually search for them. Rankings should reflect real, recent search activity rather than a static, unchanging list. The system should handle prefixes ranging from a single character up to a full phrase gracefully.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter, and the first two are really what define this whole problem.

blocks.alt: Extremely low latency, very high read throughput, relevant ranking, acceptable staleness, and high availability

blocks.text: Latency has to stay well under a hundred milliseconds, since anything slower feels laggy on every single keystroke, not just occasionally. Throughput is enormous compared to actual searches, since a single five-letter query fires five separate autocomplete requests, one per keystroke, before the user ever presses enter. Rankings need to genuinely reflect what people search for, a suggestion nobody ever actually searches is worse than useless. And critically, this system can tolerate rankings that are a few minutes stale without anyone noticing or caring, which is a much looser freshness bar than almost anything else in this document, and it is exactly what makes the architecture in section 7 so much simpler than a live-updating system would need to be.

blocks.text: This design targets a single, global ranking rather than per-user personalization, with personalization noted as a future layer in section 28. Typo tolerance is treated as a stretch feature, not core to this version. Rankings are rebuilt on a periodic, offline schedule, every few minutes rather than instantly on every single search, which this design leans into deliberately rather than fighting. Suggestions are filtered for policy-violating content and accidental personal information as part of the same offline rebuild process, before they are ever exposed live.

blocks.text: The known universe of distinct query strings, unlike the unbounded item universe in the trending topics problem, is comparatively bounded, tens of millions of distinct queries people have actually searched for historically. The number that actually dominates traffic is keystrokes, not completed searches: a single five-letter query generates five separate autocomplete requests along the way, which is why total request volume can run into the hundreds of thousands per second at peak even though the number of genuinely completed searches is a fraction of that.

blocks.text: Live traffic and ranking updates run on two entirely separate paths that barely interact. A user's keystrokes hit an autocomplete API, which queries one of several identical, read-only trie replicas, each holding the exact same in-memory trie built from the most recent offline rebuild. Separately, an offline pipeline continuously aggregates raw search logs into query frequency counts, periodically rebuilds the entire trie from scratch with those updated counts, and publishes the result as an immutable snapshot that every replica reloads on its own schedule.

blocks.text: 7.1 A Trie With Precomputed Top Suggestions
blocks.content: 7.1 A Trie With Precomputed Top Suggestions

blocks.text: The trie itself is an ordinary prefix tree, one node per character along a path from the root. What makes it fast enough for this problem is that every node additionally caches its own top handful of completions, precomputed once during the offline rebuild, rather than being computed by walking every descendant of that node on each live request.

blocks.alt: Each node along the path for a prefix like "how" caches its own precomputed top five completions, so a live query is answered by a single lookup, not a live traversal of every matching word

blocks.text: This pipeline is where all of the actual computational work happens, entirely disconnected from the latency-sensitive live query path. Raw search logs are aggregated into counts, the whole trie is rebuilt with those updated counts, and every node's cached top suggestions are recomputed as part of that same rebuild.

blocks.text: The decision to precompute each trie node's top suggestions during the offline build, rather than computing them on the fly per request, is the single choice that makes this whole system's latency numbers possible. Computing a prefix's top completions live would mean walking every word beneath that node on every single keystroke, for every user, which simply does not fit inside a hundred-millisecond budget at the request volumes in section 6.

Search logs feed a frequency aggregator, which drives a full trie rebuild recomputing every cached suggestion, ending in a freshly published snapshot

blocks.text: The happy path is exactly the live query flow above, a single lookup against already-computed data. The workflow worth walking through separately is what happens to a genuinely new, previously unseen query as it grows in popularity over time. The first time anyone searches it, it does not exist in the trie at all, since the trie only reflects what existed as of the last rebuild. As more people search it, it accumulates frequency in the search logs, and at the next scheduled rebuild it enters the trie for the first time, potentially already ranked fairly high if its early volume was substantial, all without requiring any special-cased "new term" handling anywhere in the live query path.

blocks.text: In a real sense, the entire trie is a cache, every single value it can return was computed ahead of time, and a live query never triggers any computation beyond a simple tree walk. The most heavily hit, extremely short prefixes, single letters especially, are also good candidates for an additional edge cache layer in front of the trie replicas entirely, since their result sets barely change between rebuilds.

blocks.text: Because the trie is entirely read-only between rebuilds, replica instances can be comparatively small and numerous rather than large and few, since there is no write coordination overhead to amortize across bigger machines. blocks.text: Rolling out a new trie snapshot should validate the rebuild's output against basic sanity checks, such as a minimum expected node count, before replicas are allowed to load it, since a broken or partial rebuild silently loading into production would degrade every single autocomplete request at once. Replica reloads should be staggered rather than simultaneous, so a bad snapshot is caught by monitoring after affecting only a fraction of traffic rather than all of it immediately.

from typing import Dict, List, Optional


# One node in the trie, caching its own precomputed top suggestions
# so a live query never needs to traverse its descendants.
class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children: Dict[str, "TrieNode"] = {}         # one child per next character
        self.cached_top_suggestions: List[str] = []          # this node's precomputed top completions


def _format_list(items: List[str]) -> str:
    return "[" + ", ".join(items) + "]"


# A prefix tree built offline from query frequency data, answering live
# lookups by returning a node's already-computed top suggestions.
class AutocompleteTrie:
    def __init__(self, top_k: int):
        self._root = TrieNode()                                   # the empty-prefix starting point
        self._top_k = top_k                                          # how many suggestions to cache per node
        self._query_frequencies: Dict[str, int] = {}                    # query text -> its aggregated frequency

    # Called during the offline build, once per known query and its
    # aggregated frequency, inserting it along every prefix of itself.
    def insert_query(self, query: str, frequency: int) -> None:
        self._query_frequencies[query] = frequency   # remember this query's frequency for ranking
        current = self._root                            # start walking from the root
        for c in query:
            if c not in current.children:
                current.children[c] = TrieNode()   # create the path as needed
            current = current.children[c]
            self._consider_for_top_k(current, query)   # this node might need to cache this query

    # Keeps a node's cached suggestions sorted by frequency descending,
    # trimmed to the configured top K, recomputed fully during each build.
    def _consider_for_top_k(self, node: TrieNode, query: str) -> None:
        if query not in node.cached_top_suggestions:
            node.cached_top_suggestions.append(query)   # only add once per node, even if inserted multiple times
        node.cached_top_suggestions.sort(key=lambda q: -self._frequency_of(q))   # highest frequency first
        if len(node.cached_top_suggestions) > self._top_k:
            node.cached_top_suggestions = node.cached_top_suggestions[: self._top_k]   # trim to top K

    def _frequency_of(self, query: str) -> int:
        return self._query_frequencies.get(query, 0)   # this query's known frequency, zero if somehow unknown

    # Called live, on every keystroke, walking down to the node for this
    # exact prefix and returning whatever is already cached there.
    def get_suggestions(self, prefix: str) -> List[str]:
        current: Optional[TrieNode] = self._root   # start walking from the root
        for c in prefix:
            current = current.children.get(c)          # follow this character's path
            if current is None:
                return []   # this prefix has never been searched
        return current.cached_top_suggestions   # already precomputed, no work left to do


if __name__ == "__main__":
    trie = AutocompleteTrie(3)   # cache the top 3 suggestions per node

    # Build the trie from a set of known queries and their aggregated search frequencies.
    trie.insert_query("how to code", 100)
    trie.insert_query("hot dog recipe", 95)
    trie.insert_query("how are you", 90)
    trie.insert_query("how to cook", 80)
    trie.insert_query("how to draw", 60)
    trie.insert_query("how to dance", 40)

    print(f"Suggestions for 'h': {_format_list(trie.get_suggestions('h'))}")
    print(f"Suggestions for 'ho': {_format_list(trie.get_suggestions('ho'))}")
    print(f"Suggestions for 'how': {_format_list(trie.get_suggestions('how'))}")
    print(f"Suggestions for 'hot': {_format_list(trie.get_suggestions('hot'))}")
    print(f"Suggestions for 'xyz' (never searched): {_format_list(trie.get_suggestions('xyz'))}")

    h_suggestions = trie.get_suggestions("h")
    how_suggestions = trie.get_suggestions("how")
    top_is_highest = str(how_suggestions[0] == "how to code").lower()
    print(f"Top suggestion for 'how' is the highest frequency match: {top_is_highest}")
    print(f"'hot dog recipe' appears for the broader prefix 'h': {str('hot dog recipe' in h_suggestions).lower()}")
    print(f"'hot dog recipe' correctly excluded once the prefix narrows to 'how': {str('hot dog recipe' not in how_suggestions).lower()}")
